'''Charles Vernon''' "'''Chuck'''" '''Shank''' (born July 12, 1943) is an American physicist, best known as the director of the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] from 1989 to 2004.

==Early life and education==
Charles Vernon (Chuck) Shank was born in [[Mount Holly, New Jersey]], on July 12, 1943.<ref name="LA Times">{{cite news |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |title=Lawrence Berkeley Lab Gets New Chief |date=March 18, 1989 |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-03-18-mn-151-story.html |access-date=January 21, 2016 }}</ref><ref name="ACAP">{{cite web |url=https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?shankc |title=Charles Shank |publisher=Array of Contemporary American Physicists |accessdate=January 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304104528/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?shankc |archive-date=2016-03-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="janiella">{{cite web |url=https://www.janelia.org/people/chuck-shank |title=Chuck Shank |publisher=Janelia Research Campus |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref> He entered the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he earned his [[Bachelor of Science]] (B.S.) degree in 1965, his [[Master of Science]] (M.S.) in 1966, and his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (Ph.D.) in 1969, all in [[electrical engineering]],<ref name="Physics@Berkeley">{{cite web |url=http://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/charles-shank |title=Charles Shank (E) |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref> writing his doctoral thesis on "Nonlinear Wave Interaction Spectroscopy",<ref>{{cite thesis |url= http://oskicat.berkeley.edu/record=b14301387~S1 |title=Nonlinear Wave Interaction Spectroscopy |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 |year=1969 }}</ref> under the supervision of Steven E. Schwartz.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=59377 |title=Chemistry Tree – Charles V. Shank Details |publisher=Chemistry Tree |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref>

== Career ==
After graduation, Shank joined the staff of the [[Bell Laboratories]] as a researcher. He would remain there for 20 years,<ref name="janiella" /> becoming head of its Quantum Physics and Electronic Research Department in 1976, and director of its Electronics Research Laboratory in 1983.<ref name="ACAP" /> Shank introduced the use of short laser pulses to study ultrafast events, ones that take place in a [[femtosecond]], and is considered to be the founder of [[ultrafast science]]. He pioneered the field of [[femtochemistry]], developing its techniques and technologies, and laser communications, and is the co-inventor of the [[distributed feedback laser]].<ref name="Step Down"/><ref name="DOE"/> He studied the femtochemistry of [[rhodopsin]], a photosensitive pigment found in the eye that is an important component of the mechanism of human vision. But since many chemical reactions take place in femtoseconds, ultrafast science found uses in chemistry, biology, physics, materials science, medicine, meteorology and manufacturing.<ref name="janiella"/><ref name="DOE"/>

Shank became the director of the  [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] in 1989. Under his directorship, the laboratory pursued a diverse range of initiatives, usually in cooperation with other agencies. Through the [[National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center]], he made the laboratory a locus for [[supercomputing]]. Working with the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] and the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], he helped create the [[Joint Genome Institute]] to work on the [[Human Genome Project]]. Through this joint effort the complete sequences of Chromosomes [[Chromosome 5 (human)|5]], [[Chromosome 16 (human)|16]] and [[Chromosome 19 (human)|19]] were mapped. The laboratory's SuperNova Acceleration Probe (SNAP) formed part of the [[Joint Dark Energy Mission]] to explore [[dark energy]] in collaboration with [[NASA]], and it worked with the [[University of California, San Francisco]]'s [[Comprehensive Cancer Center]] to study the disease. He strongly supported [[nanoscience]], and was co-author of ''Complex Systems: Science for the 21st Century'' (1999), in which it was an important theme.<ref name="Step Down"/><ref name="DOE"/>

In 1989 Shank was a member of the [[California Council on Science and Technology]]. The following year he was a member of the National Critical Technologies Panel in the [[Office of Science and Technology]].<ref name="ACAP"/> In this role he helped identify the most critical technologies required to  advance the United States' national security and economic prosperity. He chaired the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]]'s  Committee on Optical Science and Engineering, and was the co-author of ''Harnessing Light: Optical Science and Engineering for the 21st Century'' (1998). He was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]]' Air Force Studies Board, and of the [[Central Intelligence Agency]]'s Intelligence Science Board.<ref name="DOE"/>

Shank retired from the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory in 2004, and became a professor of chemistry, physics, electrical engineering, and computer science at the University of California, Berkeley.<ref name="ACAP"/> {{As of|2015}}, he is a member of the advisory board of the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory. He remains a professor emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley, and is a member of campus advisory boards. He is also a senior fellow at the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]'s [[Janelia Research Campus]].<ref name="LBL Advisory Board">{{cite web |url=http://www.lbl.gov/lab-leadership/advisory-board/members/#CharlesV.Shank |title=Advisory Board Members |publisher=[[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref>

== Accolades ==
Over the years, Shank received a number of accolades and awards. He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1984, the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1983, and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and is a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the [[American Physical Society]], the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE), and the [[Optical Society of America]].<ref name="Step Down">{{cite web |url=http://www.ucop.edu/news/archives/2004/feb09a.htm |title=Charles Shank to Step Down As Berkeley Lab Director |publisher=University of California Office of the President |date=February 9, 2004 |accessdate=January 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070702161928/http://www.ucop.edu/news/archives/2004/feb09a.htm |archive-date=July 2, 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was awarded the [[Optical Society of America]]'s [[R. W. Wood Prize]] in 1981,<ref name="LBL Advisory Board" /><ref name="Chem">{{cite web |url=http://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/emeriti/shank |title=Charles V. Shank |publisher=College of Chemistry, [[University of California, Berkeley]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref> the [[Franklin Institute]]'s [[Edward Longstreth Medal]] in 1982, the IEEE's Morris E. ds Award in 1983 and [[David Sarnoff Award]] in 1989), the University of California's Distinguished Engineering Alumnus Award in 1990, the International Society for Optical Engineering's Edgerton Award in 1990,<ref name="Chem"/> the [[American Physical Society]]'s [[George E. Pake Prize]] in 1996,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www2.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/Pake-prize.html |title=Charles Shank Receives Pake Prize |publisher=[[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref>  and [[Arthur L. Schawlow Prize in Laser Science]] in 1997,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/schawlow.cfm |title=Arthur L. Schawlow Prize in Laser Science |publisher=[[American Physical Society]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref> the  Optical Society of America's [[Charles Hard Townes Award]] in 2002,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/awards/award_description/charlestownes/ |title=Charles Hard Townes Award |publisher=[[Optical Society of America]] |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref> and the [[United States Department of Energy]]'s [[Enrico Fermi Award]] in 2014.<ref name="DOE">{{cite web |url=http://science.energy.gov/fermi/award-laureates/2010s/shank/ |title=Charles V. Shank, 2014 |publisher= [[United States Department of Energy]] Office of Science |accessdate=January 21, 2016 }}</ref>
